EXTRA CLASS · DOCTOR VISIT

A gentle guide for kids.

A whole check-up, one calm card at a time: the visit runs in order — getting ready, meeting the helpers, the check-up itself and after the visit — with a teddy bear on every step. Every lesson below is step by step, right on this page.

HOW THIS CLASS WORKS

A whole check-up, one calm card at a time.

The Doctor Visit is a bonus class, kept beside the main learning path: the regular classes stay the core sequence, and this one is for families with a check-up coming up — or with a child who asks "what happens at the doctor?" It helps children know what to expect by walking the visit in order, and a teddy bear comes along on every step: checked, weighed, listened to and proudly discharged, right beside your child.

The cards run in visit order on purpose. The gentle steps come first — the appointment, the waiting room, the helpers’ hello — and the two big ones, the x-ray and the hospital bed, arrive late, when your child already knows the story. Nothing at a check-up is a punishment: the doctor is counting what is already good, and the last card of the day is a proud wave goodbye.

THE VISIT, IN ORDER

From the appointment to the goodbye.

Twenty-two cards in four groups, exactly the order a check-up happens. Every step-by-step lesson is right here on this page — the original artwork beside the teaching, card after card.

Getting ready

The visit starts before the doctor says hello: the appointment, the reception desk, the name tag, the waiting room.

AppointmentReception DeskName TagWaiting Room
Meeting the helpers

The doctor and the nurse say hello first — and the scale and the exam bed are just things to stand on and sit on.

DoctorNurseWeigh-InExam Room
The check-up

The listening, the looking and the checking — one step at a time, and the doctor counts what is already good.

Check-UpStethoscopeThermometerEar CheckMouth CheckEye ChartDeep BreathX-Ray
After the visit

The part that feels like a job well done: medicine only from a grown-up, a small bandage, clean hands, and the great-job walk home.

MedicineBandageHand-WashingHospital BedFeel-BetterGoodbye
THE CLASS GAME

Play doctor at home.

Let your child be the doctor and check their teddy with a toy stethoscope — hello first, then the heart listen, the ears, the big open "aah" and one deep breath. Then swap, and your child is the patient who knows exactly what each step feels like. A child in the doctor’s seat is a child who stops worrying about the waiting room.

THE ONE RULE, SAID KINDLY

Medicine is only taken from a grown-up.

The medicine card carries the rule right on its face, and the class repeats it the same way every time: grown-ups measure it, grown-ups give it — only from a grown-up. Medicine is not candy and not a toy; it lives up high, and the child’s job is the asking: "may I have my medicine, please?" Said kindly and often, the rule becomes one the child recites without being asked — which is exactly how it protects them.

DOCTOR VISIT LESSON · DOCTOR VISIT · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Appointment — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the appointment as a plan on the calendar: the visit becomes something counted down to, not something that happens to a child.

What is this?

An appointment is the agreed time for the check-up — a day, a time and a doctor, written where the family can see it.

What does it mean?

Surprises are what make check-ups hard. A child who has crossed days off a calendar walks in already owning the visit: this was planned, and plans are safe.

What does the child need to know?

You need the appointment card, a real calendar and a crayon. Circle the day together. Every morning after, cross one more day off — a countdown any two-year-old can run.

Why this matters

The countdown does the emotional work days in advance. The morning of the visit there is nothing left to explain — the plan is simply finished, and off you go.

What it teaches

Time words (today, tomorrow, two more sleeps), anticipation managed in small doses, and the first experience of "planning" as a family skill.

Words to learn

appointmentcalendartodaytomorrowplanvisit

Say this to your child

“"Appointment! A time to visit the doctor. See — the calendar says today. We planned this! Teddy is coming too. Let’s go keep our plan."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "an appointment is a time to visit the doctor."
  2. Find the real day on the calendar and circle it together.
  3. Cross off each day as it passes — "two more sleeps!"
  4. The night before, pack with the child: teddy, the waiting-bag, socks with dinosaurs on them.
  5. In the morning: "appointment day! The plan says today."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "appointment — a time to visit the doctor" sit over a parent and child walking along, teddy under one arm, beside a calendar marked TODAY.

Ask your child

"What day is our appointment?" "Who comes with us?" "What do we pack the night before?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might circle every day on the calendar "just in case," pack the teddy a week early, or announce "appointment day!" to the whole street.

Out in the real world

Dentists, haircuts, grandma’s birthday — every one of them lives on the same calendar. The countdown trick works at all of them.

Try it together

Calendar Countdown: a paper chain with one ring per day; each morning the child pulls one off. One ring left means appointment day. The pulling is the therapy.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where does the visit live?" (on the calendar) "What do we cross off?" (the days) "Who comes with us?" (me — and teddy)

Staying safe

An appointment is a plan, never a warning. Say the day warmly — the tone a child hears on the calendar page is the tone they bring to the clinic.

This lesson pairs with the Appointment flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Doctor Visit.

DOCTOR VISIT LESSON · DOCTOR VISIT · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Reception Desk — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the reception desk as the visit’s front door: one friendly hello, one name, and the waiting begins.

What is this?

The reception desk is the desk at the front of the clinic where a helper greets families and lets the doctor know you have arrived.

What does it mean?

The desk is where a stranger becomes a helper with a face. Children who have rehearsed "hello, we are here" walk in as participants, not packages.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and a possible script: "hello, we are here — this is [name]." That is the whole line. The child says any part of it they like, even just the name.

Why this matters

First impressions run both ways: a child who has greeted the room settles faster, and a settled child makes every later step — the scale, the stethoscope — easier.

What it teaches

Social scripts (greeting, answering "who is here?"), speaking to new adults from a safe distance, and the pride of having a job at the desk.

Words to learn

reception deskreceptionisthelloarrivecheck inname

Say this to your child

“"Reception desk! We tell the receptionist our name. Hello — we are here! She will tell the doctor, and the doctor will be so happy to see you."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "the reception desk is where we say we have arrived."
  2. Rehearse the line at home: "hello, we are here!" — with a wave.
  3. At the real desk, let your child say their own name if they want to; whisper it to you is also fine.
  4. Point out the helper’s name tag and read it together.
  5. Then: "now we wait for our turn" — and on to the waiting-room lesson.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "reception desk — we tell the receptionist our name" sit over a child and parent at a curved front desk, the receptionist waving from behind a computer.

Ask your child

"Who sits at the reception desk?" "What do we say when we arrive?" "Whose name does the helper wear on a tag?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might practice the hello in the car the whole way there, hand over a toy "appointment card," or whisper the name like a secret password.

Out in the real world

Every office has a front desk — the library, the pool, the dentist. The same hello works at all of them, and it gets easier every time.

Try it together

Front Desk: a table, a toy phone, a notebook. Every stuffed animal arrives and checks in by name; your child is the receptionist — then swap, and now the child arrives and the grown-up greets. Both sides of the desk, both jobs practiced.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we do at the desk?" (say hello — we are here) "Who is behind the desk?" (a helper) "What happens after the hello?" (we wait for our turn)

Staying safe

Never promise "the receptionist will be nice" as a deal — describe what happens: we say hello, she says hello. Routines, not bargains, are what hold steady in new rooms.

This lesson pairs with the Reception Desk flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Doctor Visit.

DOCTOR VISIT LESSON · DOCTOR VISIT · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Name Tag — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the name tag as the visit’s introduction: the helpers read the tag, say the child’s name kindly, and the visit starts as a friendship.

What is this?

A name tag is a sticker or paper with your child’s name on it, so every helper in the room can greet them by name.

What does it mean?

Hearing your own name spoken warmly by a new grown-up is a small miracle for a three-year-old. The tag makes sure it happens — and the child sees exactly why.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card, paper, a marker and tape. The child draws, you write the name, teddy gets one too. Wear them to breakfast. The tag does its job before the real visit ever comes.

Why this matters

The name tag lesson is really a name-power lesson: a child who can say, spell and wear their own name brings a piece of home into the clinic.

What it teaches

Name recognition and early letters, identity pride ("that is MY name"), and reading social glue — helpers wear names too, so everyone knows everyone.

Words to learn

name tagnameletterreadwearhello

Say this to your child

“"Name tag! It helps people know your name. Look — the doctor has a tag too. Everybody reads everybody’s name, and now we are all friends."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "a name tag helps people know your name."
  2. Make one at home: the child decorates, you write the name big.
  3. Read the letters: "A… L… E… X!" Point at each one.
  4. Make one for teddy. Wear them somewhere fun — dinner, the park.
  5. At the clinic, point at the helpers’ tags: "they wear names too!"

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "name tag — it helps people know your name" sit over a nurse in scrubs handing a small tag to a child who holds a teddy bear in the other arm.

Ask your child

"What does the name tag say?" "Who else wears a name tag?" "How does the doctor know your name?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might wear the homemade tag for days, make one for every stuffed animal, or spell the name aloud to strangers at the store.

Out in the real world

Name tags are everywhere: shops, parties, library story time. Every one is a chance to practice "that is a name — it helps people say hello."

Try it together

Tag Factory: a basket of paper tags, crayons and tape. Tag everything — teddy, dog, the plant, dad. The child plays "who are you?" reading each tag aloud. Reading practice wearing a costume.

Understanding check

Ask: "Why do we wear a name tag?" (so people know your name) "What is on a tag?" (a name) "Does the doctor wear one too?" (yes — read it!)

Staying safe

A first name only on any tag that leaves the house. The privacy rule children learn here — names yes, addresses no — is worth teaching young.

This lesson pairs with the Name Tag flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Doctor Visit.

DOCTOR VISIT LESSON · DOCTOR VISIT · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Waiting Room — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the waiting room as a pause with a shape: we sit, we play quietly, our name gets called — and the visit begins.

What is this?

The waiting room is the room with chairs where families sit until the doctor is ready — the pause between the front desk and the exam room.

What does it mean?

Waiting is the hardest part of the visit because it has no edges. Giving it a job (the waiting bag), a voice level (quiet voices) and an end (your name gets called) builds those edges in.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and a "waiting bag": one small book, one quiet toy, chosen by the child the night before. The bag ONLY comes out at clinics — that is its magic.

Why this matters

A child with a waiting job does not count minutes. And the name being called — the signal they are practicing for — turns waiting into a game with a finish line.

What it teaches

Delayed gratification in tiny doses, quiet-voice practice, and the social rules of shared spaces: chairs are for sitting, inside voices, other people are waiting too.

Words to learn

waiting roomwaitturnquietcall our namepatient

Say this to your child

“"Waiting room! We wait for our turn. Read your book, hug your teddy… and when they call your name — up we go! Your turn!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "the waiting room is where we sit for our turn."
  2. Pack the waiting bag together — the child chooses one book, one toy.
  3. Play "waiting room" at home: sit in a row, read, then call the teddy’s name — teddy jumps up!
  4. At the real clinic: book out, voices low, and "when they call your name, we go in."
  5. When the name comes: celebrate the finish line — "your turn!"

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "waiting room — we wait for our turn" sit over a child sitting calmly on a blue clinic chair, teddy bear on the lap, a heart picture on the wall.

Ask your child

"What do we do in the waiting room?" (wait for our turn) "What is in the waiting bag?" "What happens when they call your name?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might pack and repack the waiting bag nightly before a visit, call everyone’s name like a receptionist, or ask "how many waits?" — which means they are counting, which means they are coping.

Out in the real world

Restaurants, the barber, the airport — waiting rooms are everywhere. The waiting bag earns its keep at every single one.

Try it together

The Great Wait: set a two-minute timer; the family waits with the waiting bag, quietly, together. When it dings — "your turn!" and the child gets called in to "see the doctor" (a mirror and a toy stethoscope). Waiting, rehearsed.

Understanding check

Ask: "What room do we wait in?" (the waiting room) "What do we do there?" (read, hug teddy, wait) "How do you know it is your turn?" (they call your name)

Staying safe

Never say "it will be quick" — quick is a promise you do not control. Say what you DO control: "we have your book, and your name will be called."

This lesson pairs with the Waiting Room flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Doctor Visit.

DOCTOR VISIT LESSON · DOCTOR VISIT · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Doctor — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the doctor as a person, not a white coat: someone who says hello, asks teddy how he feels, and takes gentle care of you.

What is this?

A doctor is the helper trained to keep bodies healthy — they look, listen and check, and they explain everything in child-sized words.

What does it mean?

The white coat and the strange room disappear when the doctor becomes a character: the person who knelt down, said hello and listened to the teddy’s heartbeat first.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and the community-helpers cards if you have them. The doctor card sits with the nurse card: two helpers, one team. Say their names, look at their smiling faces.

Why this matters

A child who can describe the doctor — "she listens to my heart, she looks in my ears" — has already organized the visit into known parts. Unknown parts are the only scary parts.

What it teaches

Helper vocabulary (who does what), trust in new adults built through description, and the social script of the medical hello.

Words to learn

doctorhelperhealthyhellocheckgentle

Say this to your child

“"Doctor! A doctor helps you feel better. She will kneel down and say hello — maybe to teddy first! She looks, she listens, she takes gentle care of you."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "a doctor helps you feel better."
  2. Notice the picture: the doctor kneels down to say hello — doctors come to your height.
  3. Introduce the team: "the doctor and the nurse work together."
  4. Play the hello: a stuffed-animal doctor greets every patient warmly before checking anything.
  5. Before the real visit: "the doctor will say hello to you — and maybe to teddy first!"

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "doctor — a doctor helps you feel better" sit over a doctor kneeling down and waving hello to a child holding a teddy bear, both smiling.

Ask your child

"What does the doctor say first?" (hello) "What is the doctor’s job?" (help you feel better) "Who does the doctor check first — you or teddy?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might assign the doctor a whole backstory ("she has a dog named Buddy"), insist teddy goes first for everything, or practice the doctor’s hello in a white shirt.

Out in the real world

The doctor also checks on babies, grandmas and even the school soccer team — everyone has a doctor, and every one of them started as a kid meeting theirs.

Try it together

Doctor’s Round: the child in a white shirt visits every "patient" in the house — hello first, questions second, check-up third. The hello-before-touching rule is the lesson, learned by playing it.

Understanding check

Ask: "Who is the doctor?" (a helper) "What does the doctor do first?" (says hello) "What is the doctor’s job?" (keeping you healthy)

Staying safe

Never use the doctor as a threat ("the doctor will give you a shot if you don’t behave"). The doctor is a helper, full stop — threats build the exact fear we are teaching away.

This lesson pairs with the Doctor flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Doctor Visit.

DOCTOR VISIT LESSON · DOCTOR VISIT · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Nurse — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the nurse as the visit’s caring expert: the one who measures, asks, wraps and reassures — often the very first face your child meets.

What is this?

A nurse is a helper trained to care for people — they weigh, measure, ask how you feel, and take gentle care of the small things at every visit.

What does it mean?

Nurses do most of the "first touches" of a visit: the scale, the questions, the bandage. A child who knows the nurse arrives expecting the friendliest part of the day.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and the teddy hospital props: toy thermometer, toy bandages. The nurse card sits beside the doctor card — one team, two sets of gentle hands.

Why this matters

Nurses are the pattern for all kindness-with-competence: firm hands, soft voice, everything explained. Naming the nurse gives your child a person to look for — "where is the nurse?" is a much better question than a worry.

What it teaches

Helper vocabulary, care-giving pretend play (nursing is empathy with props), and question-answering with a safe grown-up nearby.

Words to learn

nursecaremeasurebandagekindteam

Say this to your child

“"Nurse! A nurse helps care for you. She weighs you, measures you, asks how you feel — and she knows all about bandages. She and the doctor are a team."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "a nurse helps care for you."
  2. List what nurses do: weigh you, measure how tall, ask how you feel, wrap a bandage.
  3. Open the teddy hospital: the child is the nurse, teddy is the patient.
  4. The nurse asks teddy: "how do you feel today?" — and waits for the answer.
  5. Swap roles: now the grown-up nurses, and the child says how THEY feel — the real skill, practiced.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "nurse — a nurse helps care for you" sit over a nurse in blue scrubs kneeling beside a child sitting on a chair, teddy bear close, both smiling.

Ask your child

"Who weighs you at the clinic?" (the nurse) "What does the nurse ask you?" (how you feel) "Who works with the doctor?" (the nurse — a team)

What your child can say or do

Your child might nurse every injury in the house for a week, take teddy’s "temperature" at dinner, or ask whether the real nurse has a teddy too.

Out in the real world

Nurses work at the clinic, the hospital, the school — and they visit new babies at home. Almost every child meets a nurse before they meet a doctor.

Try it together

Teddy Hospital: admissions desk, bandage station, a thermometer, and one discharging ceremony ("all better — go home!"). Your child runs the whole hospital. The vocabulary sticks because the patients never complain.

Understanding check

Ask: "Who is the nurse?" (a helper who cares for you) "What does the nurse do first?" (weighs, asks how you feel) "Who is on the doctor’s team?" (the nurse)

Staying safe

Nurses carry needles sometimes — do not pretend otherwise if your child asks. "Sometimes nurses do a quick pinch; it is fast, and I will hold your hand." Honest beats surprised.

This lesson pairs with the Nurse flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Doctor Visit.

DOCTOR VISIT LESSON · DOCTOR VISIT · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Weigh-In — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the weigh-in as the growth report: stand on the scale, hold still, and hear how much bigger you are than last time.

What is this?

A weigh-in is standing on the clinic scale so it can measure how much your body weighs — one of the numbers that shows the doctor you are growing.

What does it mean?

Numbers about bodies are just facts — unless nobody explains them. "You grew!" is the only interpretation a three-year-old needs, and it makes the scale a scoreboard.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and any bathroom scale. Practice stepping on, standing still (the hard part!), stepping off. Weigh teddy. Weigh everyone. Numbers become a party trick.

Why this matters

The weigh-in is the first "hands-on" moment of most visits and it is completely gentle — a guaranteed early win that carries courage into the stethoscope part.

What it teaches

Measuring as describing (not judging), body-awareness vocabulary (heavier, taller, growing), and standing-still control — a real motor skill.

Words to learn

weigh-inscalestand stillgrowheavynumber

Say this to your child

“"Weigh-in! Stand on the scale — click! Hold still like a statue… and there it is: you GREW. That is the best news the doctor could hear."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "the scale checks how much you weigh."
  2. Home practice: step on, statue-still, three seconds, step off.
  3. Weigh the whole family — and teddy. Laugh at the numbers.
  4. The magic sentence: "you grew! Last time you were smaller."
  5. At the real visit: "statue time!" — and the nurse gets a perfect weigh-in.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "weigh-in — the scale checks how much you weigh" sit over a nurse guiding a child onto a clinic scale, teddy bear waiting on the floor.

Ask your child

"What does the scale tell us?" (how much you weigh) "What does it mean when the number is bigger?" (you grew!) "How do we stand on it?" (still, like a statue)

What your child can say or do

Your child might weigh everything with batteries (no) or without (also no), demand weekly weigh-ins, or announce "I GREW" to the dinner table.

Out in the real world

The market scales fruit and the bathroom scales the whole family — scales are everywhere, and every one is just a measuring machine with a job.

Try it together

The Statue Scale: painter’s tape square on the floor; whoever stands still longest "gets weighed" (a paper number held up). Best statue wins the biggest number. Silly, and it drills the exact skill.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we do on the scale?" (stand still) "What does the scale measure?" (how much you weigh) "What did the number show?" (that you grew!)

Staying safe

Keep it light and skip comments about weight in any direction other than growing. The scale measures, the doctor reads, the child hears only "you grew."

This lesson pairs with the Weigh-In flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Doctor Visit.

DOCTOR VISIT LESSON · DOCTOR VISIT · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Exam Room — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the exam room as the doctor’s own room: a bed to sit on that crinkles, a small sink, a poster on the wall — all of it expected, none of it strange.

What is this?

The exam room is where the check-up happens: an exam bed covered in paper, the doctor’s tools on the wall, and a chair for the grown-up.

What does it mean?

Rooms feel big when they are unknown. Every named object — the paper bed, the crinkle, the sink — shrinks the room to a set of ordinary things that make sounds.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and a couch cushion. The crinkle is the star: paper tablecloth, baking sheet, or actual wrapping paper — make the sound, name the sound, laugh at the sound.

Why this matters

The exam bed is usually the first thing the child meets in the real room. A child who has sat on a "crinkle bed" at home climbs straight up at the clinic — position wins half the check-up.

What it teaches

Sound-tolerance through play (crinkle = funny), room-mapping vocabulary, and the sitting-and-waiting posture the exam itself will ask for.

Words to learn

exam roomexam bedpapercrinklesinkposter

Say this to your child

“"Exam room! This is where check-ups happen. Sit on the big bed — CRINKLE! It talks! Teddy sits next to you, and the doctor will be right in."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "this is where check-ups happen."
  2. Name the furniture: exam bed, sink, poster, stool.
  3. Make the crinkle sound at home and make it funny — "the bed talks!"
  4. Build an exam room: cushion bed, teddy patient, paper "poster."
  5. At the real room: "the crinkle bed! Just like the card. Climb up."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "exam room — this is where check-ups happen" sit over a child sitting on an exam bed covered in paper, teddy bear in the lap, a heart poster on the wall.

Ask your child

"What room does the check-up happen in?" (the exam room) "What sound does the paper bed make?" (crinkle!) "Who sits next to you?" (teddy — and me)

What your child can say or do

Your child might crinkle every piece of paper in the house announcing "exam bed!", assign teddy the bed and take the chair, or ask if the real room has a poster of hearts.

Out in the real world

The exam room is also where grandpa gets his knee checked and where new babies are weighed — it is the doctor’s office, and its door opens for everyone.

Try it together

Crumple Choir: everyone gets a sheet of paper; the conductor points and the paper crinkles loud or soft. The sound that startles in a quiet clinic becomes an instrument here — mastered, owned, funny.

Understanding check

Ask: "What happens in the exam room?" (the check-up) "What sound does the paper make?" (crinkle) "Where does teddy sit?" (next to you, in the middle)

Staying safe

The exam bed is high — one hand on the child at all times in the real room, no exceptions, teddy positioned away from the edge. Say it the same way at home: "teddy sits in the middle."

This lesson pairs with the Exam Room flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Doctor Visit.

DOCTOR VISIT LESSON · DOCTOR VISIT · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Check-Up — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the check-up as a story with a shape: the doctor looks in, listens to, and counts up everything that is already going right.

What is this?

A check-up is the doctor’s full look-over: ears, mouth, heart, breath, tummy — every check is a way of seeing how the child is growing.

What does it mean?

"Check-up" sounds mechanical; "the doctor counts what is already good" sounds like a compliment. Same actions, different story — and the story is what the child feels.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and the order of the set: after the helpers say hello, the checking begins — stethoscope, thermometer, ears, mouth, eyes, one deep breath. The cards ARE the running order.

Why this matters

Children do best with sequences they can narrate. "First she listens to my heart, then my ears, then I say ah" gives the child a script to follow instead of a flow of surprises to endure.

What it teaches

Sequencing (first, then, last), body-part vocabulary in context, and cooperation as a skill the child performs proudly rather than endures.

Words to learn

check-uplistenlookcheckhealthygrow

Say this to your child

“"Check-up! The doctor looks and listens and counts what is already good: a strong heart, clean ears, big bright eyes. Everything is growing just right."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "a check-up keeps you healthy."
  2. Tell the order with the cards: heart, temperature, ears, mouth, eyes, deep breath.
  3. The frame: "the doctor is counting what is already good."
  4. Teddy gets the full check-up in order — narrate each step.
  5. At the real visit, whisper the running order: "heart now… ears next… then the big ah!"

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "check-up — a check-up keeps you healthy" sit over a doctor listening with a stethoscope to a child on an exam chair, teddy bear close by.

Ask your child

"What is a check-up?" (the doctor looking and listening) "What comes first?" (the heart listen) "What is the doctor counting?" (what is already good)

What your child can say or do

Your child might run check-ups on the whole family at bedtime, demand "count what is good" instead of a song, or narrate their own body parts like a tour guide.

Out in the real world

Check-ups happen for teeth (the dentist), eyes (the optician) and even cars (the mechanic!) — everything with a body or an engine gets a look-over now and then.

Try it together

The Growing Report: after each pretend check, the doctor announces one "already good" thing — "strong legs! bright eyes! a loud laugh!" The report ends with a sticker. Every body leaves the exam proud.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is a check-up for?" (to see how you grow) "What does the doctor check?" (heart, ears, mouth, eyes, breath) "Is anything wrong at a check-up?" (no — counting what is good)

Staying safe

A check-up is not a punishment and never framed as one — no "be good or the doctor will look in your ears." The visit counts what is good; the tone at home decides whether the child believes it.

This lesson pairs with the Check-Up flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Doctor Visit.

DOCTOR VISIT LESSON · DOCTOR VISIT · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Stethoscope — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the stethoscope as the heart’s audience: the doctor wears it to hear the boom-boom, and every child has one worth hearing.

What is this?

A stethoscope is the tool the doctor wears around the neck — the round disc listens to the heart and the breath through the skin.

What does it mean?

A cold disc on warm skin is a two-second surprise. A child playing the listening game expects the touch, names the sound, and the surprise becomes the best part of the visit.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and any toy stethoscope — or a paper tube. Listen to a real heartbeat through it, then practice the statue-still pose the real listening needs.

Why this matters

The heart listen is the centerpiece of most check-ups. A child who knows boom-boom is the goal sits tall for the disc — they are delivering the sound, not receiving a procedure.

What it teaches

Body awareness (the heart lives in the chest and never stops), cause and effect (move fast — boom-boom faster), and stillness as a skill with a purpose.

Words to learn

stethoscopelistenheartboom-boombreathdisc

Say this to your child

“"Stethoscope! The doctor listens to your heart. Boom-boom, boom-boom — hello, heart! Stand still and let the doctor hear how strong you are."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "a doctor listens to your heart."
  2. Find the heart: hand on the chest — "boom-boom, all day and night, never stops."
  3. Run in place ten steps — now listen: faster! Bodies are amazing.
  4. Paper-tube listening: your heart, their heart, teddy’s heart.
  5. At the visit: "statue still — the doctor wants to hear YOUR boom-boom."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "stethoscope — a doctor listens to your heart" sit over a child wearing a stethoscope around the neck, teddy bear beside, both ready to listen.

Ask your child

"What does the stethoscope hear?" (the heart — boom-boom) "Where does the disc go?" (on the chest, over the heart) "What happens when you run?" (the heart goes faster)

What your child can say or do

Your child might wear a toy stethoscope to breakfast, listen to the dog’s chest, or report "my heart is LOUD today" — correct, and proud of it.

Out in the real world

Doctors, nurses and midwives all carry stethoscopes; paramedics wear them around their necks on the job. The tool is the badge of the whole helping crew.

Try it together

Heart Radio: the child is the radio host broadcasting "the boom-boom show" — interviews with the heart after running, after resting, after a big laugh. Broadcasting is listening with a microphone.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the doctor hear?" (your heart) "What is the sound?" (boom-boom) "How do we help the doctor listen?" (stand still like a statue)

Staying safe

The disc feels cold for a second — say so. "It is a little chilly, then it warms up." Predicted sensations do not startle; surprises do.

This lesson pairs with the Stethoscope flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Doctor Visit.

DOCTOR VISIT LESSON · DOCTOR VISIT · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Thermometer — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the thermometer as the body’s measuring stick: a quick tick, a little beep, and the doctor reads the number.

What is this?

A thermometer measures how warm the body is — under the arm, in the ear or across the forehead, depending on which one the clinic uses.

What does it mean?

The thermometer appears at every sick day AND every check-up. A child who has played with a toy one — measuring teddy, measuring the bath — meets the real one as an old acquaintance.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and any home thermometer (bath ones count). The word is the treasure: ther-MOM-e-ter, four claps, said like a chant until the child owns it.

Why this matters

The long name is the whole game. A child who can say "thermometer" walks into any clinic holding a piece of the grown-up vocabulary — and vocabulary is confidence.

What it teaches

Measurement as a concept (hot, warm, cold — with numbers attached), syllable-clapping for the long word, and sitting-still for a count of ten.

Words to learn

thermometertemperaturewarmmeasurebeeptick

Say this to your child

“"Thermometer! It checks your temperature. Tick… tick… BEEP! All done. The doctor reads the number and smiles — just right."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "the thermometer checks your temperature."
  2. Clap the word: ther-MOM-e-ter — four claps, three times fast.
  3. Measure everything warm: the bath, teddy’s paw, your child’s forehead.
  4. The beep is the prize: "beep! All done. What does it say?"
  5. At the visit: statue still, count to ten, and wait for the beep together.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "thermometer — it checks your temperature" sit over a child with a thermometer in reach and a teddy bear looking on.

Ask your child

"What does the thermometer measure?" (how warm you are) "What sound says all done?" (the beep) "Can you say the word?" (ther-MOM-e-ter!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might clap-chant the word at random hours, "take the temperature" of soup and bathwater, or ask what number the bath got.

Out in the real world

Thermometers live in kitchen drawers (the meat one), bathroom cabinets and the car dashboard — everything warm gets measured somewhere.

Try it together

The Beep Game: any toy that beeps becomes the thermometer; the patient waits ten quiet seconds for the beep, then the number is announced with great ceremony. Ten seconds of stillness, purchased with a beep.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does it measure?" (your warmth) "What says all done?" (the beep) "How do we help?" (hold still and count to ten)

Staying safe

Only grown-ups use real thermometers — the child’s job is statue-still. Toys and bath thermometers are fair game for small hands.

This lesson pairs with the Thermometer flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Doctor Visit.

DOCTOR VISIT LESSON · DOCTOR VISIT · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Ear Check — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the ear check as a one-second wonder: a tiny light looks inside the ear while the child holds still like a statue.

What is this?

An ear check is the doctor looking into the ear canal with a small flashlight called an otoscope — gentle, quick and painless.

What does it mean?

Anything that touches the face gets the full attention of a three-year-old. Naming the tool, the light and the count — "one-two, done" — turns a flinch into a statue contest.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and a flashlight. Look at ears at home — outside only, never deep — then practice the statue pose: chin still, eyes forward, three whole seconds.

Why this matters

The ear check is over faster than the child can worry about it — IF they hold still. The statue game gives the stillness a job and a finish line.

What it teaches

Stillness control (the hardest motor skill of the visit), face-touch tolerance built at home, and trust that grown-up words match grown-up actions ("one second" means one second).

Words to learn

ear checklightotoscopestillstatuequick

Say this to your child

“"Ear check! The doctor looks inside your ear — a teeny tiny light. Hold still like a statue… one… two… ALL DONE. You did it!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "the doctor looks inside your ear."
  2. Flashlight play: light on teddy’s ear, on the wall — the light is tiny and friendly.
  3. The statue game: chin still, eyes forward, count to three — done!
  4. The script: "a tiny light, one-two, done."
  5. At the real visit: whisper "statue time" and count it out loud with the doctor.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "ear check — the doctor looks inside your ear" sit over a doctor holding a small lit otoscope to a child’s ear while the child hugs a teddy bear.

Ask your child

"What does the doctor look inside?" (the ear) "What does the doctor hold?" (a tiny light) "How long does it take?" (one-two, done)

What your child can say or do

Your child might flashlight everything at bedtime, demand ear checks for the whole family, or hold a perfect statue pose with visible pride.

Out in the real world

Ear checks happen at every check-up and every earache — the same tiny light, the same one-two. Familiar now, familiar forever.

Try it together

Statue Museum: the family poses; the "doctor" inspects ears with a flashlight and awards prizes for the stillest statue. Movement loses, stillness wins — the exact rule of the real exam.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the doctor use?" (a tiny light) "How long does the ear check take?" (one-two, done) "What is your job?" (statue still)

Staying safe

Flashlights at home stay OUTSIDE the ear — look at the outside only. The doctor is the one who looks in, and never deeper than the doctor’s gentle one second.

This lesson pairs with the Ear Check flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Doctor Visit.

DOCTOR VISIT LESSON · DOCTOR VISIT · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Mouth Check — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the mouth check as a performance the child already knows: open wide, say "aah," show the doctor what strong teeth and a busy tongue you have.

What is this?

A mouth check is the doctor looking at the teeth, tongue and throat while the child opens wide and holds the "aah" sound.

What does it mean?

Every toddler is a professional "aah"-er — tooth-brushing taught them. The mouth check is the same skill with a new audience; the mirror at home is the rehearsal space.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card, a mirror and a toothbrush. Practice the big open "aah" — wide as a lion, long as a song — then check every stuffed animal’s teeth.

Why this matters

The mouth check is the visit’s most cooperative moment when it is practiced and its most avoidant when it is not. Two mirror sessions buy a perfect real one.

What it teaches

Oral motor control (holding an open jaw), the self-care link (the same open-wide that gets teeth brushed), and performing a skill for a new grown-up.

Words to learn

mouth checkopen wideaahteethtonguelion

Say this to your child

“"Mouth check! Open wide and say AHHH. The doctor sees your teeth and your tongue — what a big lion mouth! Well checked, well done."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "open wide and say ah."
  2. Mirror practice: lion mouth — wider! Wider! Hold it.
  3. Sing the "aah" — long, short, squeaky. Make it a game.
  4. Check the toys: "open wide, teddy! What strong teeth."
  5. At the visit: "lion mouth for the doctor — big and brave!"

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "mouth check — open wide and say ah" sit over a doctor looking into a child’s wide-open mouth while the child holds a teddy bear on the lap.

Ask your child

"What do we say at the mouth check?" (aah!) "How wide does the mouth open?" (lion-wide) "What can the doctor see?" (teeth and tongue)

What your child can say or do

Your child might hold lion-mouth at random moments for days, "aah"-check the whole family after dinner, or brush teddy’s teeth with real diligence.

Out in the real world

The dentist says "open wide" too, and so does the school nurse on check-up day. The lion mouth works at all of them.

Try it together

Lion School: the child teaches the toys to open wide — "wider, teddy! Perfect aah!" Then a graduation: every animal earns a "well checked" sticker. Teaching the skill is owning the skill.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we do for the mouth check?" (open wide, say aah) "How big?" (lion-wide) "What does the doctor see?" (your teeth and tongue)

Staying safe

Only the doctor or dentist looks deep in the mouth — the home game stays at lion-mouth distance. Tongue depressors are the doctor’s tool; the home version needs nothing but "aah."

This lesson pairs with the Mouth Check flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Doctor Visit.

DOCTOR VISIT LESSON · DOCTOR VISIT · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Eye Chart — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the eye chart as a wall game: the doctor points, your child points the same way — with eyes doing the work, not words.

What is this?

An eye chart is the poster on the exam-room wall with rows of letters and pictures; the child covers one eye and points the way each one faces.

What does it mean?

Most three-year-olds cannot name letters — the chart knows that. The pictures (house, heart, hand) and pointing answers exist exactly for them, and pointing is a game every child can win.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and paper. Draw four shapes — heart, star, cup, sun — then call them out for pointing: "where is the star?" Both eyes first, then the pirate patch game: one eye covered.

Why this matters

The eye test is the visit’s quiet game — no touching, no tools, just pointing. A child who has played it at home sits on the stool like it is their own game show.

What it teaches

Direction words (up, down, left, right), shape vocabulary, and one-eye-at-a-time tolerance — the patch is the only strange part and it is practiced here.

Words to learn

eye chartpointpicturedirectioncover one eyesee

Say this to your child

“"Eye chart! We read letters and pictures with our eyes. Which way does it point? Show it with your finger — one eye, then the other. You SEE so well!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "we read letters and pictures with our eyes."
  2. Home chart: draw four shapes on paper, point and name them.
  3. The pirate round: cover one eye with a cupped hand — "now where is the star?"
  4. Swap eyes. Laugh at how funny everything looks.
  5. At the real visit: "the wall game! Show the doctor your pointing."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "eye chart — we read letters and pictures with our eyes" sit over a doctor pointing at a chart of letters while a child sits on a stool holding a teddy bear.

Ask your child

"What hangs on the wall?" (the eye chart) "How do we answer?" (point with a finger) "Which eye goes first?" (one — then the other, like a pirate)

What your child can say or do

Your child might make an eye chart for the dog, point-shape-call at breakfast, or practice the pirate patch on every doll in the house.

Out in the real world

Eye charts hang in school nurses’ offices too — the same pointing game returns every year of childhood, and it never stops being winnable.

Try it together

Chart Show: the child draws the chart and runs the game for the family — "point to the heart! Now the sun!" Doctor of charts, caller of shapes, master of directions.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is on the chart?" (letters and pictures) "How do we play?" (point the way) "What do we cover?" (one eye, then the other)

Staying safe

Never make covering an eye a punishment or a test the child can fail. It is a pointing game — and both eyes are champions at home before the chart ever asks.

This lesson pairs with the Eye Chart flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Doctor Visit.

DOCTOR VISIT LESSON · DOCTOR VISIT · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Deep Breath — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the deep breath as a two-part trick: breathe in like smelling a flower, out like blowing a candle — and the doctor hears exactly what she needs.

What is this?

A deep breath is a slow breath in through the nose and a long breath out — the doctor asks for it during the listening part of the check-up.

What does it mean?

A slow out-breath is the body’s own calm button. Teaching it for the doctor quietly hands the child a tool for every hard moment after: the dark bedroom, the big feelings, the long wait.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and imagination. Flower (cup the hands, sniff sniff) then candle (pursed lips, looooong blow). Five rounds is a full game. That is the whole skill.

Why this matters

The doctor listens MORE when the breath is slow and deep — and the child can hear the difference in their own chest. Cooperation here feels like a superpower, because it is one.

What it teaches

Breath control (a real regulation skill), imagination pairing (flower, candle), and the first experience of calming a body on purpose.

Words to learn

deep breathsmellblowflowercandleslow

Say this to your child

“"Deep breath! Breathe in and out slowly. Smell the flower… blow the candle… again! The doctor hears your wind — what a strong, slow breath."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "breathe in and out slowly."
  2. The flower: hands cupped, sniff sniff sniff — breathe in.
  3. The candle: lips small, looooong blow — breathe out. Not too fast, or the candle laughs!
  4. Five rounds, then listen: hand on the chest, "feel the wind?"
  5. At the visit: "flower… candle…" — and the stethoscope gets its best listen.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "deep breath — breathe in and out slowly" sit over a doctor listening with a stethoscope while a child sits calmly on the exam bed, teddy bear beside.

Ask your child

"How do we breathe in?" (smell the flower) "How do we breathe out?" (blow the candle) "When does the doctor ask for a deep breath?" (while listening)

What your child can say or do

Your child might flower-and-candle at bedtime unprompted, coach the whole family through five rounds, or blow out every imaginary candle in the house.

Out in the real world

The same trick works at birthday candles, soup that is too hot and big feelings at bedtime — one skill, a thousand candles.

Try it together

Candle Factory: line up ten imaginary candles; blow them out one at a time, slowly, then relight them with a sniff of a flower. The child who can light and blow ten candles owns the calm-down.

Understanding check

Ask: "How do we breathe for the doctor?" (slow — flower in, candle out) "Why slow?" (so the doctor hears the wind) "When else does the trick work?" (any big feeling)

Staying safe

Breathing games are always gentle — no breath-holding contests. In means sniff, out means blow, and dizziness means stop and rest. Say the rule once, keep it.

This lesson pairs with the Deep Breath flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Doctor Visit.

DOCTOR VISIT LESSON · DOCTOR VISIT · AGES 3–5 YEARS

X-Ray — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the x-ray as a special camera: it takes a picture of the bones inside the body, it never touches, and it is over in one click.

What is this?

An x-ray is a machine that takes a picture of the inside of the body — bones show up bright white, and taking the picture does not hurt at all.

What does it mean?

"Camera" is the word that does the work. Children know cameras: you hold still, it clicks, you see the picture. An x-ray is that — pointed at bones instead of smiles.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and (if you can) a printed hand x-ray. Count the finger bones, wave back at them, and play the statue-camera click game.

Why this matters

Most check-up children never meet the x-ray at all — but the big machine in the hallway is visible from the waiting room, and mysteries breed worry. A named camera is just furniture.

What it teaches

Inside-the-body curiosity (bones, the skeleton — a favorite preschool topic), stillness as photo-taking, and machine-vocabulary that demystifies big hospital equipment.

Words to learn

x-raycamerabonespictureinsideclick

Say this to your child

“"X-ray! It takes a picture inside your body. Look — those are your BONES! The camera never touches you. Hold still… click… all done."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "it takes a picture inside your body."
  2. Camera play: hold up fingers as a camera, "click!" — the child freezes like a photo.
  3. Show a hand x-ray if you have one: count the finger bones, wave at them.
  4. The sentence that matters: "the camera never touches you."
  5. If a real x-ray ever comes: "photo time — hold still for the bones’ picture!"

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "x-ray — it takes a picture inside your body" sit over a doctor and a child looking together at an x-ray picture of a chest on a screen.

Ask your child

"What does the x-ray take a picture of?" (your bones) "Does it touch you?" (never) "What is your job?" (hold still for the click)

What your child can say or do

Your child might x-ray everything with finger-cameras, count bones at dinner, or ask whether the bones wave on the picture.

Out in the real world

Dentists x-ray teeth, hospitals x-ray arms and legs, airports x-ray suitcases — cameras that see inside are everywhere, doing quiet, useful work.

Try it together

Bone Photo Studio: the child is the camera operator; dolls and teddies pose ("hold still… click!") and each "picture" is announced — "strong leg bones! wiggly tail bones!" Cameras are for celebrating what is already there.

Understanding check

Ask: "What kind of machine is the x-ray?" (a camera) "What does it picture?" (the bones inside) "Does it hurt?" (no — it never touches you)

Staying safe

The word x-ray never pairs with hurt, shot or owie — it is a camera and only a camera. If a real one comes, the grown-up word is still just "picture."

This lesson pairs with the X-Ray flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Doctor Visit.

DOCTOR VISIT LESSON · DOCTOR VISIT · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Medicine — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the medicine rule that outlives every visit: medicine helps the body heal, and it is taken only from a grown-up — measured and given by them, every time.

What is this?

Medicine is what helps a sick body get better — the doctor or pharmacist says how much, and a grown-up gives it exactly that way.

What does it mean?

Children learn rules as sentences they can recite. "Only from a grown-up" is short, true, and repeated at every medicine moment until the child is the one saying it.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and the rule, said the same way every time: grown-ups measure it, grown-ups give it. Real medicine lives up high. Toy medicine stays pretend. No exceptions, stated kindly.

Why this matters

This is the safety line of the whole set. Medicine mistakes at home are real and preventable, and the prevention is a three-year-old who recites the rule without being asked.

What it teaches

Safety rules as recitable sentences, the distinction between medicine and candy (same shelf, different rules), and the child’s role: asking first, always.

Words to learn

medicinegrown-uprulemeasuredoseheal

Say this to your child

“"Medicine! Take it only from a grown-up. Grown-ups measure it, grown-ups give it — and then it helps your body do its healing work."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and read its words together: "take it only from a grown-up."
  2. The two-part rule: "grown-ups measure it, grown-ups give it."
  3. Practice asking: "may I have my medicine?" — the asking is the child’s job.
  4. Where medicine lives: up high, away from toys, never in the play kitchen.
  5. Say the rule at every real medicine moment — the child repeats the last half.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "medicine — take it only from a grown-up" sit over a grown-up giving a child a small medicine cup while a teddy bear watches.

Ask your child

"Who gives medicine?" (only a grown-up) "What do you say if you want it?" (may I have my medicine, please) "Is medicine candy?" (never — it is medicine, with its own rules)

What your child can say or do

Your child might recite the rule to grandma unprompted, "prescribe" pretend medicine with perfect rules, or catch a toy rule-breaker and correct them sternly.

Out in the real world

Vitamin gummies, cough syrup, grandma’s pills — all medicine, all grown-up-given. The rule does not bend for candy-shaped anything.

Try it together

Pharmacy Rules: the play store sells "medicine" boxes, and every sale requires the buyer to say the rule out loud — "only from a grown-up!" No recitation, no sale. The rule becomes the game’s currency.

Understanding check

Ask: "Who gives you medicine?" (a grown-up — only) "What do you say first?" (may I have my medicine) "Is medicine a treat?" (no — it is healing, with rules)

Staying safe

If medicine ever looks like candy, the rule still wins — and the medicine moves higher. When the child recites it unprompted, celebrate it like a diploma.

This lesson pairs with the Medicine flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Doctor Visit.

DOCTOR VISIT LESSON · DOCTOR VISIT · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Bandage — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the bandage as teamwork: the bandage keeps the spot clean, and the body — the real hero — does the quiet healing underneath.

What is this?

A bandage is a small soft covering for a small cut — it keeps dirt out so the skin can knit itself back together.

What does it mean?

A bandage turns an "ow" into a job half-done: cleaned, covered, healing. The ritual matters as much as the plaster — clean, stick, press, "all better," because the ritual is the comfort.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and a box of bandages. Teddies get bandaged first (paw scrapes are frequent in teddy society), then one "just because" bandage for the child — worn proudly is allowed.

Why this matters

Children who have applied ten bandages to teddies meet the real one with steady hands — theirs and the nurse’s. The skill is small; the calm it buys is not.

What it teaches

Fine motor (peeling, placing, pressing), sequencing (clean, cover, press), and the first-aid frame: helping hands, not scares.

Words to learn

bandagecutcleancoverhealall better

Say this to your child

“"Bandage! It helps a small cut heal. Clean it, stick it, press it — and your body does the healing work underneath. All better!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "it helps a small cut heal."
  2. The order, always: clean the spot first, then stick, then press.
  3. Teddy hospital: wrap paws until the peeling gets smooth.
  4. One "just because" bandage for the child — a badge, worn proud.
  5. The ending word, every time: "all better."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "bandage — it helps a small cut heal" sit over a child sitting cross-legged with a small bandage on the knee, teddy bear beside.

Ask your child

"What goes on first, soap or bandage?" (soap — clean first) "What does the bandage do?" (keeps the spot clean) "Who does the healing?" (your body — the bandage helps)

What your child can say or do

Your child might run a bandage clinic for every toy, request a "just because" bandage weekly, or explain to grandma that the body heals and the bandage helps.

Out in the real world

Kitchens, playgrounds and grandpa’s workshop all keep bandages — the same clean-cover-press works at every one of them.

Try it together

Bandage Factory: a queue of stuffed patients, each with an invented tiny scrape; the nurse cleans (a wipe), covers (a bandage), presses and discharges with "all better!" Efficiency grows; so does calm.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does a bandage do?" (keeps the cut clean) "What comes first?" (cleaning) "Who does the real healing?" (your body)

Staying safe

Real wounds get a grown-up’s eyes first — the child’s bandage game stays on toys and "just because" skin. Bleeding that soaks, gapes or does not stop is a doctor moment, said calmly.

This lesson pairs with the Bandage flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Doctor Visit.

DOCTOR VISIT LESSON · DOCTOR VISIT · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Hand Washing — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches hand washing as the visit’s perfect ending and health’s perfect habit: soap, bubbles, one alphabet song, goodbye germs.

What is this?

Hand washing is washing with soap and water for about twenty seconds — long enough to sing the alphabet — so germs on the hands go down the drain.

What does it mean?

Germs are invisible, which makes them fascinating and vague. "Wash them off with soap and they go down the drain" gives the child a picture, a job and a finish line.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card, a sink and soap. The timer is the alphabet song — front, back, between the fingers, thumbs. Bubbles are the proof: no bubbles, no done.

Why this matters

The clinic sink is right there at the end of the visit — washing before leaving is a real habit AND the calmest possible close to a morning that had a lot in it.

What it teaches

Self-care independence, sequencing (water, soap, scrub, rinse, dry), and germ-logic that supports a lifetime of the habit.

Words to learn

hand washingsoapbubblesgermsrinsedrain

Say this to your child

“"Hand washing! Clean hands help keep germs away. Soap, bubbles, scrub scrub — sing the alphabet! Rinse… and goodbye, germs. Down the drain!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "clean hands help keep germs away."
  2. Water on, soap on — now the alphabet song, hands dancing: fronts, backs, between, thumbs.
  3. The bubble check: "more bubbles than yesterday? champion!"
  4. Rinse: "bye-bye, germs — down the drain!"
  5. At the clinic: wash before leaving. At home: before eating, after the toilet, after outside.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "hand washing — clean hands help keep germs away" sit over a child washing hands at a low sink with soap suds, teddy bear watching.

Ask your child

"What do germs hate?" (soap) "How long do we scrub?" (one alphabet song) "When do we wash?" (before eating, after the toilet, after outside — and before leaving the clinic)

What your child can say or do

Your child might sing the alphabet at every sink in the county, inspect everyone’s bubbles, or announce "germs lost!" at dinner.

Out in the real world

Every sink in the world works the same way — and the alphabet song travels free. Grandpa’s house, restaurants, school: the habit packs itself.

Try it together

Germ Chase: glitter lotion (or washable paint) as "germs" on the hands; wash for one alphabet song and hunt for surviving sparkles. Repeat until the technique leaves no germs standing. Vindictive, educational, fun.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we wash with?" (soap and water) "How long?" (one alphabet song) "Where do the germs go?" (down the drain)

Staying safe

Washing is for leaving the clinic AND for everyday — not a scared ritual after every touch. Germs are washed off, not feared; soap wins, the child sings.

This lesson pairs with the Hand Washing flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Doctor Visit.

DOCTOR VISIT LESSON · DOCTOR VISIT · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Hospital Bed — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the hospital bed as a piece of clever furniture: a bed with buttons that goes up and down so someone resting can be comfy while their body heals.

What is this?

A hospital bed is a bed on wheels with buttons — it raises and lowers so a resting person can eat, read or sleep comfortably while they heal.

What does it mean?

Beds that move are fascinating, not frightening — IF nobody makes them heavy. "A cozy bed that helps you rest" plus a button story keeps the wonder and drops the weight.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and a recliner (or a pillow pile). The up-and-down is the lesson: recline the chair "like a hospital bed," tuck teddy in, press the imaginary buttons.

Why this matters

Most check-up days never meet this bed — but from a waiting room, through a doorway, it is visible, and questions are better asked at home than held in a hallway.

What it teaches

Mechanical curiosity (buttons do things — engineering joy), empathy vocabulary (rest, heal, comfy), and the honest scope: some days need it, most do not.

Words to learn

hospital bedbuttonsupdownrestheal

Say this to your child

“"Hospital bed! A cozy bed helps you rest. It goes UP with a button — and down! If ever someone needs it, the bed is there, doing its cozy job."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "a cozy bed helps you rest."
  2. The buttons: "up — for sitting up and eating. Down — for sleeping flat."
  3. Recliner practice: tuck teddy in, press the arm buttons, "beep — up! Beep — down."
  4. The scope: "some days someone needs this bed to rest and heal. Most check-up days, we never see it."
  5. Leave it there — fascination, not weight.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "hospital bed — a cozy bed helps you rest" sit over a child resting comfortably in a hospital bed with the side rail down, teddy bear tucked in close.

Ask your child

"What do the buttons do?" (up and down) "Who uses the bed?" (someone who needs to rest and heal) "Do we see it on a check-up day?" (usually not — it is there if ever needed)

What your child can say or do

Your child might button-operate every chair in the house, prescribe hospital-bed rest to sleepy pets, or explain the bed to grandma like a tour guide.

Out in the real world

Hospital beds also live in nursing homes and sometimes at home — wherever someone needs rest with a button on the side. It is furniture with a kind job.

Try it together

The Button Ward: every chair becomes a bed with imaginary buttons; the nurse admits one patient (teddy), finds the cozy angle and serves breakfast in bed. Buttons, blankets, done — wonder without weight.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the bed do?" (goes up and down) "Why?" (so resting is comfy while the body heals) "Is it a scary bed?" (no — a cozy bed with buttons)

Staying safe

If someone the child loves is ever IN one, the honest frame is exactly this one: the bed is helping them rest while their body heals — and the child can visit, wave and bring a drawing.

This lesson pairs with the Hospital Bed flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Doctor Visit.

DOCTOR VISIT LESSON · DOCTOR VISIT · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Feel Better — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the visit’s real ending: the walk home where the grown-up says the magic words — you did a great job — and the day becomes a proud story.

What is this?

Feel better is the visit’s final chapter: stickers earned, hand held, the door held open — and the specific, honest praise on the walk home.

What does it mean?

Children remember endings longest. A specific "you opened wide and held still" lands deeper than a generic "good job" — it tells the child exactly which bravery worked.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and a tradition: the same small thing after every visit — a picnic on the grass, a library stop, one balloon. Traditions turn the visit into a story with a happy ending.

Why this matters

The feel-better walk is the emotional receipt of the whole visit. Named pride today is a shorter goodbye and a calmer hello at the next appointment.

What it teaches

Pride in accomplishment (named, not generic), family ritual-building, and memory-shaping: the ending the child keeps is the one the grown-up narrates.

Words to learn

feel bettergreat jobbravewalk hometraditionproud

Say this to your child

“"Feel better! You did a great job at your check-up. You opened wide, you breathed deep, you were brave — and now, the walk home. High five!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "you did a great job at your check-up."
  2. Name the specifics after a pretend visit: "you opened wide like a lion! You held still for the light!"
  3. Invent the tradition together: one treat, one stop, one song — same every time.
  4. The high five: the visit’s full-stop punctuation.
  5. After the real visit: tell the day back at dinner — with the child as the hero.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "feel better — you did a great job at your check-up" sit over a parent and child walking home hand in hand, teddy bear under the arm, clinic door behind.

Ask your child

"What do we say after the visit?" (you did a great job) "Name one brave thing you did." (opened wide / held still / deep breath) "What is our tradition?" (ours — same every time)

What your child can say or do

Your child might narrate the visit to the answering machine, demand the tradition weekly, or hand out "great job" awards to the whole family at dinner.

Out in the real world

Every hard-and-good thing deserves a walk-home: the first swim class, the hair cut, the school play. Specific praise is the glue of proud memories.

Try it together

The Award Ceremony: at home, the child receives a paper medal "for opening wide, holding still and one mighty aah." The medal goes on the fridge. The fridge becomes the family’s wall of brave.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we say after a check-up?" (you did a great job) "Why?" (because you really did the brave things) "What comes after?" (our tradition — and home)

Staying safe

Praise honestly — if a part was hard, name that too: "the ear light felt weird and you held still anyway." Children trust praise that includes the truth.

This lesson pairs with the Feel Better flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Doctor Visit.

DOCTOR VISIT LESSON · DOCTOR VISIT · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Goodbye — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the goodbye as the visit’s closing scene: the wave at the door, the friendly "see you next time" — a circle that closes gently and completely.

What is this?

A goodbye is the wave and the kind words at the end of the visit — goodbye to the doctor, goodbye to the nurse, and home.

What does it mean?

Endings decide how the whole story is remembered. A rushed exit leaves loose ends; a practiced goodbye — wave, words, door — tells the child the visit finished exactly as it should.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and the toys. Every teddy check-up ends with the same script: "bye-bye, Doctor — see you next time!" Wave included. Repetition is the rehearsal.

Why this matters

"See you next time" quietly does future work: it frames the next appointment as an expected hello between friends, not a fresh emergency.

What it teaches

Closure rituals (why every preschool day ends the same way), social scripts for leaving kindly, and future-tense comfort — next time is a friend, not a threat.

Words to learn

goodbyewavefinishedsee you next timedoorhome

Say this to your child

“"Goodbye! The visit is finished. Wave to the doctor — bye-bye, see you next time! And home we go, hand in hand."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "the visit is finished."
  2. The script: "bye-bye, Doctor — see you next time!" Wave big.
  3. Practice with the toys after every teddy check-up — the wave becomes automatic.
  4. At the real visit: pause at the door. The wave is not optional — it is the ending.
  5. Then the walk, the hand, and the day is done.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "goodbye — the visit is finished" sit over a child and parent waving goodbye to the doctor at the clinic door, teddy bear under the arm.

Ask your child

"What do we say at the door?" (bye-bye — see you next time) "What does the wave mean?" (the visit is finished) "What comes after the door?" (the walk home)

What your child can say or do

Your child might wave goodbye to the pharmacy, the post office and every bus — the script, joyfully overapplied. Let it run.

Out in the real world

Goodbyes run the whole day: school drop-off, playdates, grandparents. The practiced wave works at all of them — and so does "see you next time."

Try it together

The Goodbye Round: every teddy check-up ends with the patient waving from the "door" and the doctor waving back — both saying the line. Two roles, one ritual, zero loose ends.

Understanding check

Ask: "How does the visit end?" (a wave and goodbye) "What do we say?" (see you next time) "Why do we always wave?" (to finish the story all the way)

Staying safe

Never sneak out of any appointment to avoid a hard goodbye — the wave, even a teary one, is the trustworthy ending. Sneaking saves a minute and charges the next visit double.

This lesson pairs with the Goodbye flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Doctor Visit.
